analogy.p: A star network is like an airline with a single hub airport: every passenger flies to the hub and then on to their destination. It is cheap to run, simple and easy to manage, but if the hub airport closes, every flight is cancelled and nobody can travel. A mesh network is like a country with a dense road network: every town can be reached through many different routes, so if one road is blocked, drivers take a different road and still arrive. It is very reliable, but building so many roads is extremely expensive and complicated to maintain. The analogy is not perfect because the 'hub' (the switch) is also usually cheap and easy to replace, and in a network, data is copied into packets which can take several routes at once.

bullets: Know what is meant by **network topology**: the way the devices (nodes) in a network are arranged and connected.
Be able to **describe and draw** a **star** topology: every device connects to a central switch.
Be able to **describe and draw** a **mesh** topology: devices have connections to several, or all, of the other devices.
Know the **advantages and disadvantages** of each topology, with a reason for every point.
Be able to **compare** the two and **recommend** one for a given scenario.
Use the linked hardware vocabulary correctly: **switch, NIC, router, WAP, transmission media**.
Be able to work out the **number of connections** needed in a mesh (higher-level maths link).
core.h: What the specification asks you to know
core.p: OCR J277 section 1.3 expects you to be able to **draw and describe the star and mesh network topologies**, and to explain the advantages and disadvantages of each. A topology is the layout of a network: which devices are connected to which. In the exam you may be asked to sketch a topology, to say what a particular device does in it, to explain what happens when a cable or the central device fails, or to recommend one for a described organisation. You must always justify your choice using the details in the scenario.

bullets: A **node** is any device connected to the network, such as a computer, printer, server or switch.
A **link** (or connection) is a cable or wireless connection between two nodes. The link is the **transmission medium**: copper cable, fibre optic or radio waves.
The **physical topology** is how devices are actually cabled; the **logical topology** is how data flows. The exam focuses on the layout you would draw.
Topology is one of the factors that affects **network performance**, along with bandwidth, number of users and transmission media.
Star and mesh are the two topologies named in the OCR GCSE specification, so you do not need to learn bus or ring in detail.
The topology a network uses is chosen by comparing **cost, reliability, performance and ease of expansion**.
Both topologies can use **wired** (Ethernet cables) or **wireless** (Wi-Fi) links.
core.p: A **network topology** is the arrangement of the devices and the connections between them in a network. Devices on a network are called **nodes**: computers, printers, servers, switches, routers and wireless access points are all nodes. The topology can be thought of as the shape of the network if you drew it as a diagram, with dots for nodes and lines for the links between them. Choosing a topology affects the **cost** (how much cable and hardware is needed), the **performance** (how fast data can travel), the **reliability** (what happens when something breaks) and how easy it is to **expand** the network.

bullets: Every device (computer, printer, server) is connected to the **central switch** by its **own dedicated cable**.
The switch receives data from one device and **forwards it only to the device it is intended for**, using the address in the data.
No device connects directly to another device; **all traffic goes through the central switch**.
The switch is usually connected to a **router**, which connects the LAN to other networks such as the Internet.
A **wireless access point (WAP)** can be connected to the switch so wireless devices join the star network.
Older networks sometimes used a **hub** in the centre, which sends data to every device; modern networks use switches because they are faster and more efficient.
Number of cables needed = **one for each device** (n devices need n cables to the switch).
Star topology is by far the **most common** LAN topology today.
core.h: Star topology: how it is built
core.p: In a **star topology**, every device on the network connects directly to a **central device**, which is usually a **switch**. Each device has its own cable from its **network interface card (NIC)** to a port on the switch, so on a diagram the network looks like a star, with the switch in the middle and the cables spreading out like rays. A school computer room, an office floor and most home networks are star networks: all the computers plug into (or connect wirelessly to) one central box. The switch is often connected to a **router**, which links the whole LAN to the Internet.

bullets: **Step 1:** the sending computer splits its data into **packets** and sends them along its own cable to the switch.
**Step 2:** the switch reads the **destination MAC address** on each packet.
**Step 3:** the switch forwards the packet **only to the port** where the destination device is connected.
**Step 4:** the receiving device accepts the packet through its NIC.
If the destination is on another network (for example a website), the switch passes the packet to the **router**.
Because each connection is separate, **one device's traffic does not slow down others** as much as on a shared cable.
Because everything passes through the switch, the **switch's capacity** (speed and number of ports) affects performance.
Data on the cable between a device and the switch can be **encrypted** in wireless networks to improve security.
core.p: When one device in a star network sends data, the data travels along that device's cable to the switch. The switch reads the **destination address** in the data (the MAC address of the receiving device's NIC), looks up which of its ports the destination is connected to, and sends the data only along that cable. Because each device has its own cable, devices do not have to share one line and many pairs of devices can communicate at the same time. This is why star networks usually have good performance and few data collisions, even when many users are active.

bullets: **One cable failing only affects one device:** if the cable to a single computer breaks, that computer loses connection but all the others carry on working, because they have their own cables.
**Good performance:** each device has a dedicated connection to the switch, and the switch sends data only to its destination, so there are fewer collisions and data transfer is fast.
**Easy to add or remove devices:** a new device is plugged into a free port on the switch without disrupting the rest of the network.
**Easy to find faults:** if one device has a problem, you only need to check its own cable and port, so troubleshooting is quick.
**Easier and cheaper to set up and manage than a mesh:** only one cable per device is needed, rather than many, and administration is centralised.
**Better security and control:** all traffic passes through one point, so the switch (and router) can be used to control and monitor the network.
**Scales well** up to the number of ports available; more switches can be linked to make a larger network.
**Wireless devices** can join through a WAP connected to the switch.
core.p: The strengths of the star topology come from the fact that every device has its own connection to the centre. Each advantage should be written with its reason: you must say not just 'it is reliable' but why it is reliable.

bullets: **Single point of failure:** if the central switch fails, **every device is cut off** from the network, because all data must pass through it.
**More cabling than some other topologies:** each device needs its own cable all the way to the switch, which costs more for large spread-out sites than a single shared cable.
**Cost of the switch:** extra expense for the central device, and for larger networks switches with many ports (or several switches) are needed.
**Performance depends on the switch:** if many devices send data at once, the central switch can become a bottleneck if it is slow or overloaded.
**Limited by the number of ports:** adding more devices than there are ports means buying more switches.
**Cable length limits:** Ethernet cables have a maximum length, so devices must be reasonably close to the switch.
**Wired star networks need physical cabling**, which can be disruptive and expensive to install in older buildings.
Compared with a mesh, there is only **one route** between any two devices (through the switch), so no alternative path if it fails.
core.p: The weakness of a star is the central device: everything depends on it. Examiners most commonly ask about this single point of failure, so make sure you can state it and explain its effect. Other disadvantages relate to cost and cabling, and again each one needs a reason attached to earn the mark; do not simply write that the star 'is expensive' without saying what makes it so.

bullets: **Full mesh:** every device is directly connected to **every other device**.
**Partial mesh:** some devices have several links to others, but not all pairs are connected; this is a cheaper compromise.
Mesh networks can be **wired** (cables between routers) or **wireless** (for example Wi-Fi mesh systems where several access points connect to each other).
**Routers** (or special nodes) in a mesh decide which route a packet should take.
Mesh is used where **reliability matters most**: parts of the Internet backbone, emergency communications and some large wireless networks.
Wireless mesh nodes pass data along from one node to the next until it reaches the destination, which extends the **range** of the network.
In a full mesh with n devices, each device needs **n - 1 connections**, so each needs a NIC or port for each link.
core.h: Mesh topology: how it is built
core.p: In a **mesh topology**, devices are connected to **several other devices**, rather than all through one central point. In a **full mesh**, every node has a direct connection to every other node. In a **partial mesh**, some nodes are connected to many others and some to only a few. Data can therefore travel across the network by **more than one route**. If one link or node fails, data can be **re-routed** along another path, so the network can keep working. The Internet is a very large partial mesh: there are many routes between any two places.

bullets: **Step 1:** the sender creates packets with the **destination address**.
**Step 2:** the packets are sent over a link to a neighbouring node.
**Step 3:** each node decides **which link to use next**, based on routing information such as the shortest or least busy path.
**Step 4:** if a link has failed, the packets are **re-routed** via other nodes.
**Step 5:** the destination collects the packets and **reassembles** the message.
In a full mesh there is a **direct link** between the sender and the receiver, so data can often travel in one hop.
Because there are many routes, traffic can be **shared across the links** (load balancing), reducing congestion.
More decision-making is needed than in a star, so mesh nodes are **more complex devices** and need more processing.
core.p: In a mesh network, a packet does not have to go through one central device. Each node can pass data on to its neighbours, and a **routing** decision is made about the best path to the destination. If a link is broken or busy, packets simply take a different route. Different packets from the same message may even take different routes and are reassembled at the destination. This route flexibility is why mesh networks are so resilient and why the Internet continues to work when a single cable is cut.

bullets: **Advantage - very reliable (fault tolerant):** if one cable or node fails, data can be sent by another route so the network keeps working.
**Advantage - good performance and capacity:** many links mean traffic can be shared and sent directly, so there is less congestion.
**Advantage - no single point of failure:** there is no one central device whose failure brings the whole network down.
**Advantage - can be expanded without disrupting the network**, and wireless mesh can increase coverage.
**Disadvantage - expensive:** a full mesh needs a huge amount of cabling and many NICs or ports, and more powerful routing hardware.
**Disadvantage - complex to set up and maintain:** many connections have to be installed, configured and managed.
**Disadvantage - hard to expand a full mesh:** adding one new device needs a new link to every existing device.
**Disadvantage - more equipment to look after:** more links mean more possible faults to find and fix, even though the network as a whole keeps running.
core.p: Mesh networks trade cost and complexity for reliability. When a question asks about mesh, think 'many routes' for the advantages and 'many cables and connections' for the disadvantages. Always make each point stand alone and attach a reason, because a bare label such as 'expensive' or 'reliable' earns very little on its own.

bullets: **Formula:** links in a full mesh = n(n - 1) / 2, where n is the number of devices (nodes).
4 devices: 4 x 3 / 2 = **6** links. 5 devices: 5 x 4 / 2 = **10** links. 6 devices: 6 x 5 / 2 = **15** links.
10 devices: 10 x 9 / 2 = **45** links, compared with only **10** cables in a star.
20 devices: 20 x 19 / 2 = **190** links, compared with 20 in a star.
In a full mesh, each device needs **n - 1** connections (so 9 ports or NICs for 10 devices).
In a star with n devices, you need **n** cables (plus the switch); the central switch needs at least n ports.
This is why most real mesh networks are **partial meshes**: they keep multiple routes without connecting every pair.
In an exam, show the working: write the formula, substitute, and give the answer with the word 'links' or 'cables'.
core.h: Counting the connections in a mesh
core.p: The cost of a full mesh grows very quickly with the number of devices. Between **n** devices, the number of direct links needed is **n x (n - 1) / 2**. This is because each of the n devices connects to the other (n - 1) devices, but that counts each link twice (once from each end), so you divide by 2. A star with n devices only needs **n** links to the switch, so the difference gets larger and larger as the network grows. Being able to calculate this is a good way of backing up a statement such as 'a full mesh is expensive'.

bullets: **Reliability:** star - if the switch fails, all devices lose the network; mesh - no single point of failure, data is re-routed.
**Cost:** star - one cable per device and one switch, so cheaper; mesh - many cables and more hardware, so much more expensive.
**Installation and maintenance:** star - simple and easy to troubleshoot; mesh - complex to set up and manage.
**Performance:** star - good, but depends on the switch; mesh - good because traffic can use many routes and links.
**Failure of a single cable:** star - only that one device is cut off; mesh - nobody is cut off, as data uses another route.
**Expansion:** star - plug a new device into a spare port; mesh - a full mesh needs a new link to every other device.
**Typical use:** star - schools, offices and homes (LANs); mesh - Internet backbone, critical systems, large wireless coverage.
**Number of links for 6 devices:** star = 6, full mesh = 15.
core.p: Comparison questions are common. A good answer takes one feature at a time and says how the two topologies differ, rather than just listing facts about each. Use comparative words such as 'whereas', 'however' and 'more than'.

bullets: **School or office LAN with lots of computers and a limited budget:** star, because it is cheap, easy to manage, and a cable fault only affects one computer.
**Home network:** star with a router/WAP in the centre, because it is simple and cheap to set up.
**Hospital or emergency service control room where the network must never go down:** mesh (or partial mesh), because there are alternative routes if a link fails.
**Large Internet backbone or wide-area network linking offices in several cities:** partial mesh, for reliability and multiple routes.
**Small shop with five computers:** star, because a full mesh would be unnecessarily expensive.
**Wireless coverage over a large building or estate:** wireless mesh, so access points connect to each other and extend range.
When asked to 'justify', always **link the reason to the scenario** (for example, 'because the school has 200 computers, a star is cheaper than a mesh which would need thousands of links').
If the scenario has a particular worry (cost, downtime, expansion), build your answer around it.
core.h: Choosing a topology for a scenario
core.p: To answer a recommendation question, pick **one** topology, state it clearly, and justify it with **two or three reasons from the scenario**, then acknowledge any drawback if there are enough marks. Look for clues: 'low budget' points to a star; 'cannot afford any downtime' points to a mesh (or partial mesh); 'many computers in one room' points to a star; 'connecting several sites across a wide area' points to a partial mesh.

bullets: **Network hardware:** the switch is the centre of the star; the router connects the LAN to the Internet; the NIC in each device provides the link; the WAP provides wireless access.
**Transmission media:** star networks usually use Ethernet cables (copper or fibre) or Wi-Fi; mesh networks may use cables or radio.
**LANs and WANs:** star is typical in a LAN; the Internet WAN is a partial mesh of routers.
**Network performance factors:** bandwidth, number of devices, transmission media and topology all affect speed.
**Protocols and layers:** MAC addresses are used by switches within the star; IP addresses are used by routers between networks.
**Network security:** a central switch or router in a star is a convenient place for firewalls; many mesh links can give more places to attack.
**The Internet:** the Internet works as a huge mesh, which is how it can keep working when one route fails (see the Internet and DNS notes).
**Client-server and peer-to-peer:** both models can run on a star or mesh network.
core.p: Topologies connect to many other parts of the OCR Computer Systems paper. A connection explained in one sentence can lift a good answer to a top-band answer, but only if it is relevant to the question.

exam: **Draw/label (2 to 3 marks):** star = a central switch with lines to each device; mesh = devices with lines between many of them. Label the switch and nodes, and make sure the lines connect to the correct things.
**State (1 mark):** 'A star network has a central switch to which all devices are connected.' One clear fact is enough.
**Describe (2 marks):** make two points: 'Every device is connected to a central switch (1). The switch sends data only to the device it is addressed to (1).'
**Advantage/disadvantage (2 marks):** point plus reason: 'If one cable fails (1), only that device is affected because each has its own cable (1).'
**Explain a failure (3 marks):** say what fails, the effect on devices, and why: 'The switch fails (1). No device can send or receive data (1) because all data passes through the switch (1).'
**Compare (4 marks):** use a comparison word each time: 'Star is cheaper because it needs fewer cables, whereas a mesh needs many links and is more expensive.'

**Recommend/justify (6 marks):** choose one topology, give at least three reasons tied to the scenario (cost, number of devices, downtime, location), mention a drawback and why it is acceptable, and finish with a conclusion.
**Use numbers:** if you give a formula answer, write n(n - 1)/2 and the substitution, e.g. 8 x 7 / 2 = 28 links.
**Do not say:** 'it is better', 'it is easier' or 'it is safer' without a reason.
**Always name** the device: central switch (not 'the middle computer' or 'the server'), and say 'data packets' where relevant.
**Cover both sides:** for 'discuss', include at least one advantage and one disadvantage.

mistakes.r: Only the device on that cable is disconnected. The whole network stops only if the central switch fails.
mistakes.w: In a star network, if one cable fails the whole network stops.

mistakes.r: The central switch is a single point of failure: if it fails, all devices lose connection.
mistakes.w: A star network has no single point of failure.

mistakes.r: A full mesh needs many cables and ports, so it is expensive and complex; it is the reliability that is its main advantage.
mistakes.w: A mesh network is cheap because it is simple.

mistakes.r: In a full mesh it can, but in a partial mesh data may pass through other nodes, and it is re-routed if a link fails.
mistakes.w: In a mesh, data always goes straight from sender to receiver.

mistakes.r: Say why: each device has its own dedicated connection to the switch, which sends data only to its destination, so there are few collisions.
mistakes.w: The star is better because it is faster.

mistakes.r: A switch sends data only to the correct device. A hub sends it to all devices.
mistakes.w: The hub sends data to the right computer.

mistakes.r: Mesh can be wired or wireless; it describes the pattern of connections, not the medium.
Star describes the layout. It can use cables or a WAP in the centre.
Security depends on protection such as encryption and firewalls; complexity does not by itself make it secure.
mistakes.w: Mesh is more secure because it is more complicated.

mistakes.r: The centre is normally a switch. The router connects the LAN to other networks (it may be built into the same box in a home).
mistakes.w: The router is the centre of every star network.

summary: You need to be able to describe, draw and compare the star topology (every device linked to a central switch) and the mesh topology (devices linked to several others so data has more than one route), giving the advantages and disadvantages of each and recommending one for a scenario. It matters because topology choice affects cost, performance and reliability, and appears in short and extended OCR Paper 1 questions.

terms.d: The arrangement of devices (nodes) and the connections between them in a network.
Any device connected to a network, such as a computer, printer, server, switch or router.
A network layout in which every device is connected to a central device, usually a switch.
A network layout in which devices are connected to several other devices, so data has more than one possible route.
A mesh in which every node is directly connected to every other node.
A mesh in which some, but not all, nodes are directly connected to each other.
A network device that receives data and forwards it only to the device it is addressed to.
A simple central device that sends incoming data to all connected devices (rarely used now).
A device that forwards data between different networks, for example a LAN and the Internet.
Network interface card: the hardware that allows a device to connect to a network.
Wireless access point: a device that lets wireless devices connect to a wired network.
The cables or wireless signals that carry data between devices.
A part of a system which, if it fails, causes the whole system to stop working.
The ability of a system to keep working when part of it fails.
A small unit of data sent across a network, containing the destination address and part of the message.
The amount of data that can be transferred across a network connection in a given time.
When two devices try to send data on the same line at the same time, corrupting the data.
Local area network: a network covering a small geographical area, such as a school, usually owned by one organisation.

worked.ans: (a) Star: 8 cables (1). (b) Full mesh: 8 x 7 / 2 = 28 cables (1). The company should choose a star topology (1), because it needs far fewer cables and hardware so it is cheaper and easier to set up and manage, and if one cable fails only that computer is affected (1).
worked.q: A small company has 8 computers in one office. Calculate the number of cables needed for (a) a star network and (b) a full mesh. Which topology should it choose, and why? [4 marks]
steps: (a) Star: one cable from each computer to the switch = 8 cables.
Difference: 28 - 8 = 20 extra cables for the mesh.
Choose star because a small office does not need the extra reliability of a mesh, and it is cheaper and easier to manage.

worked.ans: All 200 computers would be unable to send or receive data on the network (1) because every device is connected to the central switch and all data has to pass through it (1). The school could keep a spare switch ready to replace it, or connect devices via more than one switch so a single failure affects fewer computers (1).
worked.q: A school has a star network with a single switch connecting 200 computers. Explain what would happen if the switch failed. State one way the school could reduce this risk. [3 marks]
steps: Identify the effect: all computers lose the connection.
Give the reason: all data passes through the switch.
Give a way to reduce the risk: a spare switch or a second switch/link.

worked.ans: A mesh topology is the most suitable (1). In a mesh there is more than one route between devices, so if one cable is damaged, data is sent along another route and the network keeps working (1). This is important in a hospital because staff must always be able to reach patient records and equipment (1). A mesh is more expensive and complex to install than a star, but the higher cost is justified because a failure could put patients at risk (1).
worked.q: A hospital wants a network that keeps working even if a cable is damaged. Recommend a topology and justify your choice. [4 marks]
steps: Name the topology: mesh (full or partial).
Explain the key feature: multiple routes between devices.
Link to the scenario: patient records and equipment must always be reachable.
Mention the drawback: higher cost and complexity, which is acceptable here.
